benchmarks.name: YourMechanic (Ford Fusion)
benchmarks.note: mobile-mechanic example quotes $852.24 (2011 Fusion 3.0L) to $1,249.36 (2013 Fusion 2.0L turbo); shop/dealer comparison prices $987-$1,913. The page's stated average of $416 ($206 parts + $210 labor) does not match its own examples.

finding: The live range of $330-$1,400 is about right. Our implied totals (in-tank pump module + hours x $120-$160 per hour, the national middle used for this arithmetic) are: economy 2018 Corolla $502-$1,080; midsize 2018 Camry $433-$948; truck 2018 Tundra 5.7L $344-$1,088; luxury 2011 BMW 528i $321-$768. Across the four that is roughly $320-$1,090. The bottom matches: the cheapest cases we could build are $321 and $344, against a live floor of $330. The top we built stops near $1,090, about $300 short of $1,400, but that gap is expected and is not a reason to lower the top: every labor time here is a manufacturer recall/warranty time or a seller's approximate figure, which run shorter than what shops bill; all four example vehicles reach the pump quickly; and the same Toyota letter lists vehicles needing 2.1-3.4 hours (Highlander, Sienna, 4Runner, Land Cruiser), which with an $800 list-price module comes to about $1,050-$1,350. The outside estimates also sit toward the upper half: Kelley Blue Book $611-$894, YourMechanic $852-$1,249 for a Ford Fusion with shop/dealer prices to $1,913, and RepairPal $1,344-$1,513 (RepairPal's $1,104-$1,160 parts figure is well above any in-tank module list price we found, so it may include dearer vehicles or more than the module). Jerry is the low outlier at $374-$679. If anything the live top is slightly conservative for tank-drop vehicles at dealer prices, but the evidence here does not justify moving either end. Why parts dominate: the module's list price ($592-$840) is two to three times the quality aftermarket price ($189-$322), so the choice of part moves the total more than the labor does. Caveats: Corolla and Camry hours are a single Toyota recall time each (no second, retail figure was found, so low = high); the Tundra low of 1.0 hr is one seller's approximate install time; the BMW time is 11 BMW flat-rate units converted at 10 units per hour on the strength of a technician blog and an owner forum, not a BMW document, and if the conversion differed in 2016 the 1.1 hr would change; the recall operations replace the pump on the same access path as a full module swap. The Delphi module for the Camry is listed for the L trim only, and the Pierburg unit for the BMW was special-order. The Tundra high is the dearest of four Toyota assemblies ($660-$832 list) because the right one depends on tank size and fuel type.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or fuel-pressure test fee, a new tank seal or lock ring, a fuel pump strainer if the new unit does not include one, an in-line fuel filter where the vehicle has one (a parts-retailer how-to guide says to always replace the strainer and to replace in-line filters), shop supplies, and sales tax. On vehicles without an access panel under the rear seat the tank has to be lowered, which adds labor (one estimator states 3-4 hours against 1.5 with an access panel) and sometimes new tank straps or filler-neck hoses if the old ones are rusted. Tank cleaning is added if the old pump failed from contamination. The parts figures here are the in-tank module only; the engine-mounted high-pressure pump on direct-injection engines is a separate, dearer part ($1,200-$1,500 list on the Toyota and BMW catalog pages seen).
